mcq.q: Demand: Qd = 100 − 2P. Supply: Qs = 20 + 2P. The equilibrium price is:
mcq.explain: At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 100 − 2P = 20 + 2P, so 80 = 4P and P = ₹20. The equilibrium quantity is 100 − 2 × 20 = 60 units, and the supply side gives the same: 20 + 2 × 20 = 60. The value 60 is quantity, not price.
mcq.fast: Set Qd = Qs and solve for P.

mcq.q: Demand: Qd = 120 − 3P. Supply: Qs = 2P − 10. The equilibrium quantity is:
options: 26 units
52 units
40 units
42 units
mcq.explain: Set 120 − 3P = 2P − 10, so 130 = 5P and P = ₹26. Equilibrium quantity = 120 − 3 × 26 = 42 units; check with supply: 2 × 26 − 10 = 42. The value 26 is the equilibrium price, a common trap when the question asks for quantity.
mcq.fast: Find P first, then put it back into either equation.

mcq.q: Demand: Qd = 100 − 2P. Supply: Qs = 20 + 2P. If the price is held at ₹30, the excess supply (surplus) in the market will be:
options: 20 units
40 units
60 units
80 units
mcq.explain: At P = 30, quantity demanded = 100 − 60 = 40 and quantity supplied = 20 + 60 = 80. Supply exceeds demand by 80 − 40 = 40 units, which is the surplus. Since ₹30 is above the equilibrium price of ₹20, competition among sellers would push the price down. The value 80 is quantity supplied, not the surplus.
mcq.fast: Price above equilibrium -> surplus = Qs − Qd at that price.

mcq.q: During a festival season the demand for sweets rises sharply, while the supply conditions stay the same. Compared with before, the market will show:
options: A rise in both equilibrium price and quantity
A fall in price and a rise in quantity
A rise in price and a fall in quantity
No change in price or quantity
mcq.explain: When demand increases (the demand curve shifts right) and supply is unchanged, there is excess demand at the old price. The price rises, and the higher price draws out more supply along the supply curve, so both equilibrium price and quantity increase.
mcq.fast: Demand up -> P up, Q up.

mcq.q: Demand remaining unchanged, an increase in supply leads to:
options: A rise in both price and quantity
A fall in both price and quantity
A fall in equilibrium price and a rise in equilibrium quantity
A rise in price and a fall in quantity
mcq.explain: An increase in supply shifts the supply curve to the right. At the old price there is excess supply, so the price falls; the lower price makes buyers demand more along the demand curve. Hence the equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises.
mcq.fast: Supply up -> P down, Q up.

mcq.q: Demand and supply both increase in exactly the same proportion. As a result:
options: Price rises and quantity is unchanged
Price falls and quantity falls
Equilibrium quantity rises, and equilibrium price remains unchanged
Both price and quantity fall
mcq.explain: When both curves shift right by the same amount, the upward pressure on price from higher demand is exactly offset by the downward pressure from higher supply. Price stays the same, but quantity rises because both buyers and sellers are trading more at that price.
mcq.topic: Simultaneous changes in demand and supply
mcq.fast: Equal increases: Q up, P unchanged.

mcq.q: Demand increases by more than supply increases. The equilibrium price will:
options: Rise, and the equilibrium quantity will rise
Fall, and the quantity will rise
Remain unchanged
Fall, and the quantity will fall
mcq.explain: Both shifts raise the equilibrium quantity. For price, the stronger force wins: since the increase in demand is larger than the increase in supply, there is net excess demand at the old price, so the price rises. If supply rose more than demand, price would fall.
mcq.topic: Simultaneous changes in demand and supply
mcq.fast: Both up: Q up; price follows the bigger shift.

mcq.q: If the market price is below the equilibrium price:
options: There is excess supply, and the price tends to fall
The market is in equilibrium
Demand and supply both fall
There is excess demand, and the price tends to rise
mcq.explain: Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is excess demand or a shortage. Buyers compete for the limited goods and sellers find they can charge more, so the price rises until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied again.

mcq.q: In the market with Qd = 120 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10, a tax shifts supply to Qs = 2P − 20. The new equilibrium price is:
mcq.explain: Set 120 − 3P = 2P − 20, so 140 = 5P and P = ₹28. The price rises from ₹26 to ₹28 and quantity falls from 42 to 120 − 84 = 36 units. A decrease in supply, demand unchanged, raises price and lowers quantity.
mcq.fast: Supply down -> new P higher, new Q lower.
